title: How would you handle a database deadlock in production?
description: Understand deadlock detection, resolution, and long-term prevention in SQL Server and application code.

data.text: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions each hold a lock that the other needs, and neither can proceed. SQL Server detects deadlocks and kills one victim, but the killed transaction's client sees an error. In production, deadlocks manifest as intermittent 500 errors or retry loops that confuse users.
Interviewers want to see that you handle deadlocks on three levels: detect and recover at runtime, analyze the root cause from system views, and redesign the code or schema to prevent recurrence.

The immediate response is to catch SqlException error number 1205 (deadlock victim) and retry the transaction. The retry must be at the transaction level, not the request level, so that partial work is rolled back before retrying.

data.title: C#: EF Core deadlock retry policy

data.text: Exponential backoff is important because retrying immediately after a deadlock often recreates the same collision. The delay gives the other transaction time to complete and release its locks.

SQL Server preserves deadlock graphs in the system health extended event session. Extract the XML graph to see which resources each transaction held and requested. The graph reveals the exact tables, indexes, and statements involved.

data.title: SQL Server: Read deadlock graph from system health
data.code:
SELECT XEvent.value('(data/value)[1]', 'XML') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM (
    SELECT CAST(target_data AS XML) AS TargetData
    FROM sys.dm_xe_sessions AS s
    JOIN sys.dm_xe_session_targets AS t
        ON s.address = t.event_session_address
    WHERE s.name = 'system_health'
      AND t.target_name = 'ring_buffer'
) AS Data
CROSS APPLY TargetData.nodes('//RingBufferTarget/event') AS XEventData(XEvent)
WHERE XEvent.value('@name', 'NVARCHAR(MAX)') = 'xml_deadlock_report';

items: Access tables in a consistent order across all transactions. If Transaction A always reads Orders before Customers, and Transaction B always reads Customers before Orders, circular waits cannot form.
Keep transactions short. Move non-database work — API calls, file I/O, logging — outside the transaction scope.
Use the lowest appropriate isolation level. READ COMMITTED is usually sufficient; SNAPSHOT isolation reduces reader-writer deadlocks but adds tempdb pressure.
Add retry logic at the data-access layer, not just the controller level.
Consider application-level locks (sp_getapplock) for complex cross-resource coordination when table-level locking is too coarse.

data.text: A common interview confusion is mixing deadlocks with blocking. Blocking is one transaction waiting for another to release a lock — it is normal and resolves when the lock holder commits. Deadlocking is mutual blocking that SQL Server resolves by killing one process. Always clarify which scenario you are discussing.

data.title: Deadlock retry is not a free pass
data.text: Retry logic masks deadlocks but does not fix them. Always pair automatic retries with root-cause analysis. A system retrying the same deadlock every minute is not reliable — it is hiding a design flaw.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Catch SqlException 1205 and retry with exponential backoff at the transaction scope.
Extract the deadlock graph from system_health to identify the exact resources and statements involved.
Prevent deadlocks by accessing resources in a consistent order and keeping transactions short.
Use the lowest appropriate isolation level and monitor deadlock frequency as a health metric.
data.takeaway: Retry to recover, analyze to understand, redesign to prevent.
